conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having nausea and vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since yesterday morning. I’ve thrown up over ten times—greenish stuff, not bloody. I couldn’t keep anything down except a little ginger ale in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. Any pain, fever, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain or fever, but I feel chills and so tired. It’s like my usual gastroparesis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Your vitals show you’re a bit tachycardic and your blood pressure was high earlier, but it’s come down. We’ll start IV fluids and some anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took a compazine suppository at home—it helped a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We gave you IV compazine, Zofran, and fluids in the ER. You also got insulin since your blood sugar was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How’s my blood sugar now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable. We adjusted your insulin while you’re not eating. You’ll continue your usual Lantus at night and resume your sliding scale when you can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ve had three admissions this month—worried something’s wrong with my gastric pacer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you had it checked recently. Since then, you’ve had two more flares. Dr. Patel said unless things worsen, we’ll keep your current plan. But you can stop by his clinic any afternoon if you’re concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. What about my blood pressure? It’s been all over the place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been labile. You were on clonidine before but stopped. We’re restarting a clonidine patch—once a week. It’s better for you since you vomit so often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to pick up the prescription last time. Will I get it this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending it to your pharmacy. But you’ll need to follow up with your PCP to keep it going. We’re also adjusting your lisinopril to 7.5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. My white blood cell count was high—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 15.8, but no fever or infection signs. Likely from dehydration and stress. It’s already down to 7.0 today—back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my stomach? Any blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray—no obstruction or free air. Lungs are clear. Your gastric pacer leads are in place. So no signs of perforation or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been on Reglan at home—will I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re giving IV Reglan every six hours. Once you can eat, we’ll switch back to oral—same dose, four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since last night. I sipped some broth—kept it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll try advancing your diet to soft foods today—like toast and applesauce. Small amounts, slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have ginger ale? Regular, not diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, regular ginger ale is fine. In fact, if you’re only tolerating clear liquids at home, it’s better to have regular ones to avoid ketosis, especially with your diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that. I’ve been sticking to diet drinks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history, if you’re not eating enough, your body can go into ketosis. So regular clear liquids are okay short-term. But resume your diabetic diet when you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well today—kept down soup, crackers, and juice. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before: Protonix for GERD, Reglan four times a day, aspirin, and your insulin. Plus, we’re adding the clonidine patch for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, now 7.5 mg daily. But we’re writing it as 5 mg tablets—you’ll take one and a half each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with Dr. Patel in two weeks for your pacer. If symptoms worsen before then, you can walk in to his clinic any afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go back to clear liquids. If you can only keep those down, it’s okay to have regular ones to prevent ketosis. But if you develop fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no vomiting overnight and ate a light breakfast. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Just to confirm—I’m taking the clonidine patch weekly, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one patch weekly. And keep all your other meds. Follow up with your PCP about the patch and your blood pressure control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel chills or fatigue again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Monitor your symptoms. Fatigue and chills can be part of a flare. But if you spike a fever or feel worse, call your doctor or return here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers and prescriptions ready. You should be out by 10 a.m.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my urine test showed ketones earlier, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s why we emphasized regular clear liquids. It helps prevent your body from breaking down fat for energy when you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll watch that at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing great. Just take it slow with food and keep up with your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic if needed, but hopefully not in the hospital again soon.
